sciENE: What kind of energy is shown? A car driving down the highway
A moving car has motion energy.
What kind of energy is shown? A barking dog
Barking makes sound waves we can hear, which is sound energy.
What kind of energy is shown? A warm radiator
A warm radiator gives off heat energy that warms the room.
What kind of energy is shown? A lit flashlight
A flashlight gives off light that lets us see.
What kind of energy is shown? A skater gliding across the ice
A gliding skater is moving, so the skater has motion energy.
What kind of energy is shown? A drum being hit
Hitting a drum makes it vibrate and produce sound energy.
What kind of energy is shown? A bowl of hot soup
Hot soup holds heat energy you can feel.
What kind of energy is shown? A glowing firefly
A firefly makes its own light, which is light energy.
What kind of energy is shown? A swinging playground swing
A swing moving back and forth has motion energy.
What kind of energy is shown? A whistle blowing
A whistle makes a sound we hear, which is sound energy.
What kind of energy is shown? A heated pool on a cold day
A heated pool has warmth, which is heat energy.
What kind of energy is shown? A lighthouse beam at night
A lighthouse beam is light that ships can see.
What kind of energy is shown? A leaf blowing in the wind
A leaf moving through the air has motion energy.
What kind of energy is shown? A singing bird
A bird's song travels as sound energy.
What kind of energy is shown? A clothes iron that is turned on
A hot iron uses heat energy to smooth clothes.
What kind of energy is shown? A glowing computer screen
A computer screen gives off light so we can see it.
Which of these shows sound energy?
A ringing phone makes a sound we can hear.
Which of these shows motion energy?
A runner racing to the finish line
A runner who is moving has motion energy.
Which of these shows light energy?
A birthday candle flame lighting a dark room
A candle flame gives off light that brightens the room.
Which of these shows heat energy?
A toaster makes heat that warms and browns the bread.
Rubbing your hands together quickly makes them feel warm. What kind of energy do you feel?
Rubbing your hands creates heat energy, which makes them warm.
A rocket blasts off and roars loudly. Which kind of energy is the roar?
A roar is a sound, so it is sound energy.
sciEnTrans: A gas stove heats a pot of water. What energy change happens in the flame?
Burning gas releases stored chemical energy as heat (thermal energy).
An electric fan spins. What energy change happens in its motor?
The fan's motor turns electrical energy into the kinetic energy of the spinning blades.
A plant makes food using sunlight. What energy change happens?
Photosynthesis stores the energy of sunlight as chemical energy in sugar.
A hydroelectric dam makes power from falling water. What energy change happens in the generator?
Moving water spins turbines, and the generator turns that kinetic energy into electrical energy.
A doorbell rings when pressed. What energy change happens in the bell?
The doorbell uses electrical energy to make sound.
A microphone picks up your voice. What energy change happens?
A microphone turns sound vibrations into electrical signals.
A car's engine burns gasoline to move the car. What energy change happens?
Gasoline's chemical energy is released and turned into the car's motion (kinetic energy).
A glow stick is bent and starts to glow. What energy change happens?
Chemicals mixing inside the glow stick release energy as light.
A cyclist brakes hard and the brake pads get hot. What energy change happens?
Friction in the brakes turns the bike's kinetic energy into thermal energy.
A hand-crank flashlight is wound up. What energy change happens in its generator?
Turning the crank spins a small generator that changes kinetic energy into electrical energy.
An electric kettle boils water. What energy change happens?
The kettle's heating element turns electrical energy into thermal energy.
A phone battery is being charged. What energy change happens in the battery?
Charging stores electrical energy as chemical energy in the battery.
A ball is held high and then dropped. What energy change happens as it falls?
As the ball falls, its stored gravitational potential energy becomes kinetic energy.
A stretched slingshot is released. What energy change happens?
The energy stored in the stretched band becomes the motion of the stone.
A coal power plant burns coal to make electricity. What is the first energy change?
Burning coal first releases its chemical energy as heat.
A television is turned on. Which energy changes happen?
A TV uses electrical energy to make a picture (light) and sound.
The Sun produces energy in its core. What energy change happens there?
Nuclear fusion in the Sun's core releases energy as light and heat.
A guitar string is plucked. What energy change happens?
The vibrating string's motion produces sound energy.
A battery-powered toy car drives across the floor. What overall energy change happens?
The battery's chemical energy ends up as the toy car's motion.
A firework explodes in the sky. What energy changes happen?
The firework's chemicals release energy as light, sound and heat.
An electric heater warms a room. What energy change happens?
An electric heater turns electrical energy into thermal energy.
Solar cells on a roof power a home. What energy change happens in the cells?
Solar cells turn the Sun's light energy into electrical energy.
sciXsSeeObj: Which object is a light source?
The Sun
A full Moon
A shiny spoon
A white sheet of paper
The Sun makes its own light; the others only reflect light.
Why does green grass look green?
It reflects green light and absorbs most other colours
It makes green light
It absorbs green light
It lets all light pass through
We see the colour that an object reflects, and grass reflects mostly green light.
Which object is NOT a light source?
A mirror
A campfire
A glowing light bulb
A lightning bolt
A mirror only reflects light; it does not make its own.
Why can you read a book under a lamp?
Light from the lamp reflects off the page into your eyes
Your eyes send light out to the page
The book makes its own light
The lamp makes the words glow
We see objects when light bounces off them and enters our eyes.
Which part of the eye lets light in?
The pupil
The eyelash
The eyebrow
The eyelid when closed
The pupil is the opening that lets light into the eye.
A blue shirt is in a room with no light at all. What do you see?
Nothing, because no light reflects off it
A bright blue shirt
A glowing shirt
A white shirt
Without light there is nothing to reflect into your eyes, so you cannot see the shirt.
Why does a yellow banana look yellow?
It reflects yellow light into your eyes
It absorbs all light
It makes yellow light
It is see-through
An object's colour is the colour of light it reflects.
Which object reflects light but does not make it?
A bicycle reflector
A firefly
A candle flame
A flashlight
A bicycle reflector bounces light back but does not produce its own light.
What travels from an object to your eyes so you can see it?
Light
Sound
Air
Heat only
Light reflected or given off by an object enters our eyes and lets us see it.
Why is it easier to see a white car than a black car at night?
The white car reflects more light
The white car makes its own light
The black car reflects more light
Black cars are invisible
White surfaces reflect most light, so more light reaches our eyes.
Which object gives off its own light?
A glowing campfire
A window
A puddle
A road sign
A campfire makes its own light; the others only reflect or let light through.
Why can you see a planet like Venus in the night sky?
It reflects light from the Sun
It makes its own light
It is a star
It is on fire
Planets do not make light; they shine by reflecting sunlight.
Which surface would reflect the most light into your eyes?
A white wall
A black chalkboard
Dark soil
A black garbage bag
White surfaces reflect most of the light that hits them.
A red ball sits in sunlight. Which colour of light does it mostly reflect?
Red
Blue
Green
None at all
A red object reflects red light and absorbs most other colours.
What happens to light that hits a black car?
Most of it is absorbed
All of it is reflected
It turns into sound
It passes straight through
Black objects absorb most light, which is why they look dark and get warm.
Why do we see lightning?
Lightning gives off its own light
It reflects moonlight
It reflects light from houses
Our eyes make it glow
Lightning is a light source because it produces its own light.
How can you see your friend across a sunny playground?
Sunlight reflects off your friend into your eyes
Your friend gives off light
Your eyes shine light on your friend
Sound carries the image to you
Sunlight bounces off your friend and travels to your eyes.
Which statement about seeing is true?
We see objects when light from them enters our eyes
Our eyes give off light to see
We can see without any light
Only light sources can be seen
Seeing needs light to travel from an object into our eyes.
Why does a window look see-through?
Light passes through the glass
Glass makes its own light
Glass absorbs all light
Glass reflects all light
Clear glass lets light pass through, so we see what is behind it.
Which of these is a natural light source?
A star
A street lamp
A car headlight
A television
Stars make their own light naturally; the others are human-made.
Why do safety vests have shiny strips?
The strips reflect light so drivers can see the wearer
The strips make their own light all the time
The strips absorb light
The strips make the vest warmer
Reflective strips bounce headlight beams back toward drivers.
A cat can see in dim light but not in total darkness. Why?
Seeing needs at least some light
Cats are blind at night
Darkness is too loud
Cats see with sound
Eyes, even a cat's, need some light to enter them to see.
sciXsLightT: Clear glass lets almost all light pass through, so it is transparent.
Tissue paper lets some light through but scatters it, so it is translucent.
Which object would make the darkest shadow?
An opaque wooden block blocks all light, making a dark shadow.
What happens to light when it hits a black surface?
Black surfaces absorb most of the light that hits them.
Why does a pencil look bent when half of it is in water?
Light changes direction as it passes between water and air
Light refracts at the boundary between water and air, making the pencil look bent.
What is it called when light bounces off a surface?
Light bouncing off a surface is called reflection.
What is it called when light bends as it passes from one material into another?
Refraction is the bending of light as it enters a different material.
Why can't you see around a corner?
Light moves in straight lines, so it cannot bend around a corner to reach your eyes.
A flashlight moves closer to an object. What happens to the object's shadow on the wall?
Moving the light closer to the object blocks more light, making a larger shadow.
Which tool uses a curved piece of glass to bend light and make things look bigger?
A magnifying glass is a lens that refracts light to enlarge images.
What colours make up white sunlight?
All the colours of the rainbow
White light is a mix of all the colours of the rainbow.
Which surface gives the clearest reflection?
A calm lake is smooth, so it reflects light evenly and gives a clear image.
Why does a rough surface not show a clear reflection?
It scatters light in many directions
It bends light into a rainbow
Rough surfaces bounce light in many directions, so no clear image forms.
Wood blocks all light, so it is opaque.
What does a periscope use to let you see over a wall?
A periscope uses angled mirrors to reflect light from above the wall to your eyes.
Why does a dark shirt feel warmer in the sun than a white shirt?
Dark materials absorb more light, which turns into heat.
Which material lets some light through so you can see blurry shapes?
Frosted glass is translucent: it lets some light through but blurs it.
Light shines through a glass of water and lands slightly to the side. Why?
Light bends as it enters and leaves the water
Light refracts when it passes into and out of water, changing its path.
Why does a shadow have the same outline as the object?
Light travels in straight lines past the edges of the object
Shadows are made of dark light
Straight light rays are blocked by the object, so the shadow copies its shape.
What is the fastest that anything can travel?
Light travels faster than anything else, about 300 000 km every second.
Which is an example of transmission of light?
Sunlight passing through a clear window
Transmission is when light passes through a material, like clear glass.
At sunset, the Sun is low in the sky. What happens to the length of your shadow?
sciCND: Which of these is a conductor of electricity?
Steel is a metal, and metals let electricity flow easily.
Which of these is a conductor of electricity?
Copper is a metal and a very good conductor.
Which of these is a conductor of electricity?
Aluminum is a metal, so it conducts electricity.
Which of these is a conductor of electricity?
Gold is a metal and conducts electricity well.
Which of these is a conductor of electricity?
Brass is a metal mixture that conducts electricity.
Which of these is a conductor of electricity?
Iron is a metal, so electricity can flow through it.
Which of these is a conductor of electricity?
Metal forks are made of steel, which conducts electricity.
Which of these is a conductor of electricity?
Steel nails conduct electricity because they are metal.
Which of these is an insulator of electricity?
Rubber does not let electricity flow easily, so it is an insulator.
Which of these is an insulator of electricity?
Plastic blocks the flow of electricity, so it is an insulator.
Which of these is an insulator of electricity?
Dry wood does not conduct electricity well, so it is an insulator.
Which of these is an insulator of electricity?
Glass does not allow electricity to flow, so it is an insulator.
Which of these is an insulator of electricity?
Wool is a poor conductor of electricity, so it is an insulator.
Which of these is an insulator of electricity?
Ceramic blocks electricity, which is why it is used on power lines as an insulator.
Which of these is an insulator of electricity?
Cork does not let electricity pass through, so it is an insulator.
Which of these is an insulator of electricity?
Dry paper does not conduct electricity, so it is an insulator.
Why are electrical wires covered in plastic?
Plastic is an insulator that keeps electricity from escaping
The plastic coating is an insulator that keeps people safe from the current in the metal wire.
Why is the inside of an electrical wire made of copper?
Copper lets electricity flow easily, so it is used inside wires.
A bulb lights up when an object is placed in the gap of a circuit. What does this tell you about the object?
It is a switch that is off
If the bulb lights, electricity flowed through the object, so it is a conductor.
A bulb stays off when a rubber eraser is placed in the gap of a circuit. Why?
Rubber blocks electricity, so the circuit stays open and the bulb stays dark.
Why do electricians wear rubber gloves?
Rubber is an insulator that protects them from shocks
Rubber conducts electricity to their hands
Rubber does not let electricity flow, so it helps protect the worker's hands.
Copper, iron and aluminum are all metals, which conduct electricity.
sciCircuit: What is a complete path that electricity flows around called?
A circuit is a complete loop through which electric current flows.
Which part of a circuit changes electrical energy into light?
A light bulb turns electrical energy into light.
A circuit has a gap in the wire. What happens to the bulb?
A gap makes an open circuit, so current cannot flow to the bulb.
What is a circuit called when there is only one path for the current?
A series circuit has all parts connected in a single loop.
What is a circuit called when the current has more than one path?
A parallel circuit has branches, giving the current several paths.
Which material should be used to cover wires for safety?
Plastic is an insulator, so it keeps electricity inside the wire.
What happens when you add a second battery in series to a simple bulb circuit?
Two batteries in series give a higher voltage, pushing more current through the bulb.
What does a fuse or circuit breaker do?
Stops the current if too much flows
Adds more energy to the circuit
A fuse or breaker breaks the circuit when current gets dangerously high.
What unit is used to measure electric current?
Electric current is measured in amperes.
What unit is used to measure voltage?
Voltage, the push that drives current, is measured in volts.
What unit is used to measure resistance?
Which device measures the voltage across a part of a circuit?
A voltmeter is connected across a component to measure voltage.
Which device measures the current flowing in a circuit?
An ammeter measures current in amperes.
In a circuit, which way does conventional current flow outside the battery?
From the positive terminal to the negative terminal
From the negative terminal to the positive terminal
By convention, current is shown flowing from the positive (+) terminal to the negative (−) terminal.
Ohm's law says V = I × R. If the current is 2 A and the resistance is 3 Ω, what is the voltage?
V = I × R = 2 A × 3 Ω = 6 V.
A 9 V battery is connected to a 3 Ω resistor. What current flows?
I = V ÷ R = 9 V ÷ 3 Ω = 3 A.
What happens if a wire connects the two ends of a battery with nothing else in between?
A short circuit that can make the wire very hot
A short circuit has very little resistance, so a large current flows and heats the wire.
Two bulbs are in parallel. One is unscrewed. What happens to the other bulb?
In a parallel circuit, each bulb has its own path, so the other bulb still gets current.
Why are the lights in a classroom wired in parallel?
So each light gets the full voltage and can work on its own
So all lights go out together
Parallel wiring lets each light work independently at full brightness.
In a circuit diagram, what does a long line next to a short line stand for?
A cell is drawn as a long line (positive) next to a short line (negative).
What does a resistor do in a circuit?
Increases the voltage of the battery
A resistor opposes current, reducing how much flows.
Which change would make a bulb in a simple circuit glow dimmer?
More bulbs in series add resistance, so less current flows and each bulb is dimmer.
sciReflAbs: What happens to the light or sound? A dolphin's clicks bounce off a fish and come back.
The sound bounces back from the fish, which is reflection.
What happens to the light or sound? A soft carpet makes a room quieter.
The carpet soaks up sound energy, which is absorption.
What happens to the light or sound? You hear a friend talking through a closed door.
Sound passes through the door, which is transmission.
What happens to the light or sound? A dark rock on the beach gets hot in the sunshine.
The dark rock takes in light energy and turns it into heat, which is absorption.
What happens to the light or sound? You see the trees upside down in a calm lake.
The still water bounces light back to your eyes, which is reflection.
What happens to the light or sound? With your ear on a table, you hear a friend tapping on the far end of it.
The sound travels through the wood of the table, which is transmission.
What happens to the light or sound? Foam panels in a recording studio stop echoes.
The foam soaks up sound so it does not bounce back, which is absorption.
What happens to the light or sound? A bat hears its squeak return from a cave wall.
The squeak bounces off the wall, which is reflection.
What happens to the light or sound? Light passes through a sheet of clear plastic wrap.
Light going through a transparent material is transmission.
What happens to the light or sound? A car's headlights light up a road sign that shines back at the driver.
The sign bounces the headlight beam back, which is reflection.
What happens to the light or sound? A black solar panel takes in sunlight.
The panel takes in light energy, which is absorption.
What happens to the light or sound? Sound from a speaker travels through the air to your ears.
Sound passing through air to you is transmission.
What happens to the light or sound? Snow on the ground makes a winter day sound very quiet.
Fresh snow soaks up sound waves, which is absorption.
What happens to the light or sound? You see your face in a shiny spoon.
The smooth metal bounces light back to you, which is reflection.
What happens to the light or sound? Whales hear each other's songs through kilometres of ocean water.
Sound passing through water is transmission.
What happens to the light or sound? A pencil in a glass of water looks bent at the water's surface.
Light bends as it passes between water and air, which is refraction.
What happens to the light or sound? A magnifying glass bends light to make letters look bigger.
The lens bends light as it passes through, which is refraction.
What happens to the light or sound? A heavy winter coat in the sun warms up quickly because it is dark blue.
The dark coat takes in light energy as heat, which is absorption.
What happens to the light or sound? You hear your voice come back after shouting in an empty gym.
Your voice bounces off the walls as an echo, which is reflection.
What happens to the light or sound? Sunlight goes through a thin white curtain and lights up the room.
Light passes through the curtain, which is transmission.
What happens to the light or sound? Raindrops bend sunlight into a rainbow.
Light changes direction as it enters and leaves raindrops, which is refraction.
What happens to the light or sound? Ocean water far below the surface is dark because sunlight has been taken in by the water above.
The water takes in the light energy as it travels down, which is absorption.
sciFlower: Which thin stalk holds up the anther?
The filament is the stalk of the stamen that holds up the anther.
Which tube connects the stigma to the ovary?
The style is the stalk of the pistil between the stigma and the ovary.
What do ovules become after fertilization?
The transfer of pollen from an anther to a stigma
Pollination is moving pollen from the male anther to the female stigma.
Which part of the flower is where pollen lands to begin fertilization?
The sticky stigma catches pollen grains.
What is the main job of a flower?
Flowers are the reproductive parts of flowering plants.
Which flower part contains the male sex cells?
Pollen grains carry the male sex cells.
Which part of the flower contains the female sex cells (eggs)?
Egg cells are found inside the ovules in the ovary.
Which sweet liquid do many flowers make to reward pollinators?
Nectar is a sugary liquid that attracts bees, butterflies and hummingbirds.
Which part of the flower grows into the seed coat and seed inside a fruit?
Each fertilized ovule becomes a seed inside the fruit.
Grass flowers are small and dull with no scent. How are they most likely pollinated?
Wind-pollinated flowers do not need bright petals or scent to attract animals.
Why do wind-pollinated flowers make huge amounts of light pollen?
Most pollen blown by the wind never reaches a stigma
Pollen is food for the wind
Wind is random, so plants make lots of pollen to make sure some lands on a stigma.
Which flower part is male: the stamen or the pistil?
The stamen, made of the anther and filament, is the male part.
A bee gets pollen on its body at one flower and visits another. Which part of the second flower should the pollen land on?
Pollen must reach the stigma for pollination to happen.
Which green parts are found at the base of a flower, under the petals?
Sepals are green, leaf-like parts at the base of the flower that protected the bud.
After pollen lands on the stigma, what grows down through the style to the ovary?
A pollen tube carries the male sex cell down to the ovule.
What is it called when a male sex cell from pollen joins with an egg in the ovule?
Fertilization is the joining of a male and female sex cell.
An apple is a fruit. Which flower part did the apple mostly develop from?
Fruits develop from the ovary, which surrounds the seeds.
Which flower part has a dusty, yellow powder on it?
The anther makes and holds pollen, the yellow powder.
Why do many flowers that open at night have pale petals and strong scents?
To attract night pollinators like moths
Pale colours and scents help moths find flowers in the dark.
Pollen moving to the stigma of the same flower or plant
Pollen moving to a different species
In self-pollination, pollen comes from the same flower or plant.
Which part together with the stigma and style makes up the pistil?
The pistil is made of the stigma, style and ovary.
sciXsBeak: A flamingo's bent bill, held upside down in water, is adapted for…
A flamingo strains small shrimp and algae from water with its bill.
An owl's short, hooked beak is adapted for…

A cardinal's short, thick beak is adapted for…
A thick, strong beak gives cardinals the force to crack open seeds.
A sandpiper's long, thin beak is adapted for…
probing mud and sand for small animals

A wide gape helps swallows scoop up flying insects.
A toucan's large, light beak is adapted for…
A toucan's long beak lets it reach fruit on thin branches.
A spoonbill's flat, spoon-shaped bill is adapted for…
sweeping water to catch small animals
cracking hard seeds and nuts open
A spoonbill swings its bill through water to catch fish and shrimp.
A snake's jaw that can open very wide is adapted for…
Flexible jaws let snakes swallow animals larger than their heads.
A cow's flat, wide back teeth are adapted for…
Flat molars grind tough grass and leaves.
A wolf's long, pointed canine teeth are adapted for…
Sharp canines help wolves grip and tear prey.
A beaver's large, sharp front teeth are adapted for…
Beavers' strong incisors chew through trees for food and building.
A butterfly's long, coiled mouthpart is adapted for…
biting into tree bark for sap
A butterfly's proboscis works like a straw for drinking nectar.
A mosquito's needle-like mouthpart is adapted for…
piercing skin and sucking blood or plant juices
A mosquito's sharp mouthpart pierces skin to suck liquids.
A frog's long, sticky tongue is adapted for…
Frogs flick their sticky tongues out to snatch insects.
A blue whale's baleen plates are adapted for…
Baleen works like a sieve to strain krill from water.
A long neck on a swan is adapted for…
A swan stretches its long neck underwater to feed on plants.
A Canada goose's flat bill with tooth-like edges is adapted for…
grabbing and cutting grass and plants
The jagged edges of a goose's bill help it grip and tear grass.
A kingfisher's long, dagger-like beak is adapted for…
Kingfishers dive and grab fish with their sharp, straight beaks.
A hawk's sharp, hooked beak is adapted for…
Hawks use hooked beaks to tear the prey they catch.
A giraffe's long, grasping tongue is adapted for…
digging up roots from the soil
A giraffe wraps its long tongue around branches to strip off leaves.
A chickadee's short, pointed beak is adapted for…
picking insects and seeds from bark and twigs
A small, pointed beak lets chickadees pick up tiny insects and seeds.
A shark's rows of sharp, triangular teeth are adapted for…
Sharp, serrated teeth let sharks cut through flesh.
sciXsFeet: A duck's webbed feet are adapted for…
Webbing between the toes pushes against water like a paddle.
A cheetah's long, slim legs are adapted for…
Long, light legs let cheetahs take huge strides when sprinting.
A woodpecker's feet, with two toes forward and two back, are adapted for…
gripping the sides of tree trunks
This toe arrangement helps woodpeckers cling to bark while they drill.
A bat's wings, made of skin stretched over long finger bones, are adapted for…
A bat's arms and fingers form wings that let it fly.
A monkey's long, gripping tail is adapted for…
Some monkeys use their tails like an extra hand when climbing.
A camel's wide, padded feet are adapted for…
walking on soft sand without sinking
Wide feet spread the camel's weight over the sand.
A seal's flippers are adapted for…
Flat flippers push seals through water.
A mountain goat's split hooves with rough pads are adapted for…
The hooves spread and grip so goats can climb cliffs.
A grasshopper's large back legs are adapted for…
Strong back legs launch grasshoppers into the air.
A penguin's flipper-like wings are adapted for…
Penguins cannot fly; their stiff wings work as flippers in water.
A lynx's large, furry paws are adapted for…
Big furry paws act like snowshoes for the Canada lynx.
A badger's long, strong front claws are adapted for…
Badgers dig quickly with their powerful claws.
A squirrel's sharp claws are adapted for…
Sharp claws grip bark as squirrels climb.
An eagle's strong talons are adapted for…
Eagles snatch fish and small animals with their sharp talons.
A horse's single hard hoof on each foot is adapted for…
Hard hooves protect horses' feet as they run.
A water strider's long, thin legs are adapted for…
standing and moving on top of water
digging into mud at the bottom
climbing up the stems of plants
Long legs spread its weight so it does not break the water's surface.
A beaver's webbed back feet are adapted for…
Webbed feet help beavers swim well.
A ptarmigan's feathered feet are adapted for…
walking on snow and keeping feet warm
Feathers on the feet act like snowshoes and keep them warm.
A praying mantis's spiky front legs are adapted for…
The spiny front legs snap shut to trap prey.
A chimpanzee's hands with thumbs are adapted for…
Thumbs let chimpanzees grasp objects and branches.
A heron's long, thin legs are adapted for…
Long legs let herons stand in water while they hunt fish.
A dolphin's flippers and tail fluke are adapted for…
Flippers steer and the tail fluke pushes dolphins through water.
sciXsSkin: A polar bear's thick fur and layer of fat help it…
Fur and fat insulate the polar bear against the cold.
A zebra's stripes are thought to help it…
stay warm on cold winter nights
Scientists think the stripes confuse predators and keep biting flies away.
A duck's oily feathers help it…
A snowshoe hare's brown summer fur helps it…
blend in with the forest floor
Brown fur matches the summer ground so predators cannot see it easily.
A skunk's black-and-white fur helps it…
Bold markings warn predators about the skunk's smelly spray.
A camel's thick fur on its back helps it…
Thick fur shields the camel's body from the strong sun.
A pangolin's overlapping scales help it…
protect itself when it rolls into a ball
keep its skin wet in the sun
Hard scales act like armour against predators.
A crocodile's thick, bumpy skin helps it…
Tough, bony plates in the skin protect crocodiles.
A peacock's bright feathers help it…
Male peacocks show off their colourful tail feathers to attract females.
A lizard's dry, scaly skin helps it…
Scales reduce water loss, helping lizards live in dry places.
A sheep's thick wool helps it…
Wool traps air and keeps sheep warm.
A ptarmigan's white winter feathers help it…
White feathers hide the bird against snowy ground.
A poison dart frog's bright colours help it…
warn predators that it is poisonous
